bibliography.abstract: Marketisation reforms in China are often described as an extension of Western New Public Management (NPM), yet their meanings and effects vary substantially across regions and remain poorly understood from the perspective of policymakers themselves. Drawing on document review and interviews with sub-national officials and practitioners involved in highway maintenance in two underdeveloped provinces, this study examines how marketisation is interpreted, justified, and enacted through a "learning by doing" process shaped by administrative legacies, political incentives, and constrained market environments. The analysis shows that NPM-related principles, such as competition and performance management, are selectively adapted rather than directly transplanted, producing hybrid arrangements that combine bureaucratic control with quasi-market practices dominated by state-owned enterprises. The study identifies four narrative frames through which policymakers explain and evaluate reforms, as well as the recurring strategy of deliberate inaction, which emerges as a pragmatic response to tensions between central expectations and local socio-economic realities. It also considers the broader implications of marketisation for highway service performance, public satisfaction, fiscal sustainability, and technical capacity, pointing to uneven outcomes and persistent governance tensions. By foregrounding sub-national agency and context-sensitive adaptation, the article contributes to understanding policy transfer, the institutional logics shaping China's state-led market reforms, and the prospects for more sustainable infrastructure governance in less developed regions.
bibliography.title: “Crossing the river by feeling the stones”: Sub-national agency in China's highway maintenance marketisation

en.caveats: The findings are based on qualitative data from two underdeveloped provinces and may not represent the dynamics of highway maintenance reforms in wealthier Chinese regions.
en.what: This study analyzes how highway maintenance marketization is implemented in two underdeveloped Chinese provinces using document reviews and interviews with sub-national officials and practitioners. It identifies four narrative frames used by policymakers to justify reforms and documents how New Public Management principles are selectively adapted into hybrid arrangements that combine bureaucratic control with quasi-market practices dominated by state-owned enterprises.
en.why: It demonstrates that sub-national agency and deliberate inaction serve as pragmatic coping mechanisms when central policy expectations conflict with local socio-economic realities, challenging the assumption that Western public management reforms are directly transplanted into the Chinese administrative context.
